title: You can film the TikTok. You still need words before you can press record.
markdown:
# You can film the TikTok. You still need words before you can press record.

At 9:42 p.m., the clip is trimmed, the lighting looks good, and the sound is ready. Then the notes app opens. The cursor blinks. Ten minutes pass, then twenty, and the video that felt obvious while you were filming suddenly needs a first line, a middle, and an ending.

That stall is easy to misread as a lack of discipline. Usually it is a writing problem with a very particular shape: you know your subject, you can see the finished video, but you cannot yet turn the idea into words that make a stranger stay.

This article gives you a repeatable way to get past that blank page. It is for creators who can shoot and edit but lose momentum at the script stage. The aim is not to make every video sound polished. It is to get you a usable first draft quickly enough that you can improve it with the footage in front of you.

## Start with the moment, not the topic

"I want to make a video about meal prep" is a topic. It does not tell a viewer why this clip matters in the next second.

Start instead with the moment that made you pick up the camera. Maybe it was opening the fridge after work and finding nothing that could become dinner. Maybe it was realizing you had bought the same ingredient twice. That moment gives the script something to push against.

Write one plain sentence:

> I made this because [a specific thing happened] and I wanted [a specific result].

For example: "I made this because I kept spending money on lunch when I had food at home, and I wanted five easy lunches ready by Sunday night."

That sentence does not need to appear word for word in the final video. It gives you a point of view, which is what a blank page lacks.

## Give the viewer a reason to keep watching

Your opening does one job: it tells the right viewer that the next few seconds are for them. A useful opening is concrete enough to recognize and honest enough to deliver on.

Weak: "Here are some tips for better TikTok videos."

Stronger: "If you can edit a clean video but keep deleting the first sentence, write this part before you touch the timeline."

The stronger version names a real frustration and makes a small promise. Do not promise a viral result. Promise the next useful thing: a method, a decision, a before-and-after, or an answer to one annoying question.

## Use a three-part spine

You do not need a screenplay. You need a spine that keeps the clip from wandering.

1. **The friction:** What went wrong, felt difficult, or cost more time than it should have?
2. **The turn:** What did you try, notice, or change?
3. **The payoff:** What can the viewer do, expect, or avoid after watching?

For a video about reorganizing a tiny kitchen, the spine might read:

"I could never find the pan I needed without pulling out half the cabinet. I moved the everyday tools to one reachable shelf and stopped storing things by category. Now I can make dinner without starting with a small avalanche."

It is not literary. It is filmable. You can match each sentence to a shot.

## Write for the footage you already have

Creators often freeze because they try to invent a perfect script before looking at what they shot. Reverse that order.

Lay out your clips. Name what is visible in each one. A hand opening a package, a failed first attempt, a close-up of the result, a reaction. Then write a sentence that earns each clip its place. If a line describes something the viewer can already see, cut the line or make it add context.

For example, do not say "I am chopping onions" over a close-up of chopping onions. Say why this cut matters: "I stopped chopping everything at once because the herbs were turning slimy before I used them."

The footage carries the obvious part. Your script carries the reason, the decision, or the surprise.

## Make the first draft deliberately rough

The first version can be blunt. In fact, it should be. Write the hook, the three-part spine, and one sentence for each clip. Read it aloud once. If you stumble, shorten the sentence. If it sounds like a brochure, replace the big claim with the thing that actually happened.

Leave room for your own phrasing. A script that sounds slightly like you will survive recording better than a smooth paragraph you would never say to a friend.

## When the page is still blank

Use a prompt that asks for a draft built around your actual material, not a pile of generic hooks. Include the audience, the footage, the point you want to make, and any words you would not use. Then revise the result against the clips. You are the person who knows whether the line is true, whether the shot proves it, and whether the ending earns the opening.

## A script is a bridge to recording

You do not need to become someone who loves staring at a blank page. You need a small process that gets you to the next take.

Start with the moment. Name the friction. Put one useful turn in the middle. End where the viewer has something they can use. Then record a rough version before you talk yourself out of it.
